description: National Income is the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced by a country in a financial year. In macroeconomics, it is primarily measured using three methods: Product Method, Income Method, and Expenditure Method.

sections.title: Historical Background and Measuring Agency
sections.description: India has a rich history of estimating national income, with several notable attempts made both before and after independence.

historical_events.significance: Dadabhai Naoroji made the first estimate of India's national income in his book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'. He estimated the per capita income at Rs 20.
Dr. V.K.R.V. Rao provided the first systematic and scientific estimate of the national income of India.
Set up by the Government of India under the chairmanship of P.C. Mahalanobis, this committee laid the framework for post-independence income measurement.

important_facts.fact: Currently, the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) calculates the National Income of India.
The current base year for calculating National Income and GDP in India is 2011-12 (which was revised from 2004-05 in January 2015).

sections.title: Product Method / Value Added Method
sections.description: In this method, national income is measured by aggregating the Gross Value Added (GVA) by all productive enterprises in the economy during a year.

key_concepts.explanation: The error of counting the value of the same product more than once. It is avoided by taking only the value of 'final goods' or by summing up the 'value added' at each stage of production.
The value of goods used as raw materials and utilities in the production process. This is subtracted from the gross value of output to find the actual value added.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: GVA = Value of Output - Intermediate Consumption
scientific_principles.application: Used to measure the real production contribution of a specific sector. The sum of GVA of all sectors gives the GDP at Market Price.

sections.title: Income Method
sections.description: This method measures national income by summing up the factor incomes distributed to the factors of production (Land, Labour, Capital, and Entrepreneurship).

key_concepts.explanation: One-sided payments like pensions, scholarships, or gifts, made without any productive service provided in return. These are strictly NOT included in the national income.
Income generated from property and entrepreneurship. It includes rent, royalty, interest, and profit.

scientific_principles.principle_or_law: Net Domestic Product at Factor Cost (NDP_FC)
scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: NDP_FC = Compensation of Employees + Operating Surplus + Mixed Income of Self-Employed
scientific_principles.application: Calculates the total income generated within the domestic territory. Adding Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) to this yields the National Income.

sections.title: Expenditure Method
sections.description: This method measures the total expenditure incurred on final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of the economy during an accounting year.

key_concepts.explanation: Also known as Investment Expenditure. It includes expenditure on fixed assets (like machinery and construction) and change in inventory (closing stock minus opening stock).
Money spent on buying second-hand goods is not included in the calculation of national income, as their value was already accounted for in the year they were originally produced.

scientific_principles.application: Where C = Private Final Consumption Expenditure, I = Investment Expenditure, G = Government Final Consumption Expenditure, and (X-M) = Net Exports (Exports minus Imports).

key_associations.associated_with: Net National Product at Factor Cost (NNP_FC)
key_associations.extra_info: Technically, NNP_FC is considered the actual 'National Income' of a country. Formula: NNP_FC = NNP_MP - Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
It is considered the best and most reliable indicator of the economic growth and standard of living of a country's citizens.
It is an index that measures changes in prices of all goods and services produced. Formula: (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100.

key_concepts.explanation: Real GDP is measured at constant (base year) prices and is a true indicator of economic volume growth. Nominal GDP is measured at current prices and includes the inflated effects of price rises.
